## What's new in SBK 10.6

SBK 10.6 is a major distributed-benchmarking, runtime-efficiency, and
reliability release. It turns SBK-GEM into a self-bootstrapping cluster
launcher, dramatically reduces its default deployment payload, strengthens
fail-fast behavior from remote clients through SBM, and preserves exact
nanosecond percentile reporting with lower aggregation overhead.

### Highlight: self-bootstrapping distributed benchmarks

SBK-GEM can now take a normal SBK distribution and bootstrap a compatible
benchmark runtime across a cluster without a preinstalled SBK tree, remote
shell scripts, or manual Java setup.

- A versioned Java remote agent replaces shell-script deployment and performs
  file operations, process launch, verification, cleanup, and diagnostics
  through an explicit binary protocol.
- Remote Java is probed per target. A compatible Java 25 or newer installation
  is reused; otherwise SBK-GEM provisions a content-addressed managed runtime.
- `SBK_JAVA_HOME` is selected, persisted, propagated, and reported consistently
  by local and remote SBK applications.
- Runtime archives are digest-verified, atomically activated, protected by
  leases and heartbeats, and reused on later invocations when their content
  identity matches.
- Deployment compatibility is based on the operating system rather than an
  unnecessarily strict controller/worker architecture match. The local Docker
  qualification fixture uses a Linux controller container, so distributed
  validation also works from macOS hosts.

### Highlight: compact Java and driver-scoped SBK copies by default

The default SBK-GEM deployment no longer copies the complete controller JDK
and every enabled storage driver to every node.

- Compact mode creates a runtime-only Java image with `jlink` and packages only
  SBK core, the selected driver, and that driver's transitive runtime closure.
- Gradle emits validated per-driver manifests and pathing JARs while standard
  `build`, `installDist`, and `distTar` outputs remain complete distributions.
- `-fullcopy false` is the default. Use `-fullcopy true` when a complete JDK and
  complete SBK distribution are explicitly required on every remote node.
- Java and SBK payloads retain independent content-addressed caches, so a node
  can reuse either component without retransferring the other.
- `-packagescleanup` defaults to `true` and retires inactive older full and
  driver-scoped SBK packages across copy modes. Managed Java runtimes remain
  reusable.
- ChromaDB is excluded from the aggregate build because its all-platform local
  embedding dependency closure dominates distribution size. Its source remains
  available for an explicitly enabled ChromaDB build.

For common drivers such as File, this changes remote deployment from copying a
large all-driver distribution and full JDK into transferring a compact Java
runtime plus a much smaller driver-specific SBK package.

### Faster, more scalable SBK-GEM orchestration

- SSH sessions are still independent per node, but compatible nodes share
  Apache MINA client infrastructure by immutable security policy. A timeout or
  authentication failure cancels only the affected connection attempt.
- Control work, bulk transfers, and benchmark-duration commands use separate
  executors. Transfer concurrency scales automatically with unique remote
  targets within configurable bounds, allowing large clusters to deploy in
  bounded parallel waves.
- Physical targets are deduplicated, preventing aliases from repeating Java or
  SBK deployment work.
- Java probing starts per target rather than behind a cluster-wide barrier, and
  bootstrap directory resolution, agent verification, and installation are
  pipelined to reduce startup round trips.
- Bulk SCP reports transferred bytes, percentage, aggregate rate, ETA, pending
  hosts, temporary archive destinations, and final SBK execution directories.
- Password authentication is prioritized when `-gempass` or
  `SBK_GEM_SSH_PASSWD` is supplied. Passwordless agent/key authentication
  remains supported, with host-key behavior resolved internally for the chosen
  authentication mode.

### Strong distributed lifecycle and diagnostics

- SBK-GEM coordinates remote registration before benchmark timing begins, so
  deployment and startup do not dilute measured performance.
- Remote command failure, authentication failure, registration timeout,
  transport failure, SBM failure, and cleanup failure retain bounded host-level
  diagnostics and produce an authoritative distributed result.
- Final results clearly separate expected, successful, and failed nodes and
  report maximum SBM registration participation.
- Start time, end time, total execution duration, selected Java source, Java
  home, runtime reuse/copy decisions, and remote SBK installation paths are
  logged explicitly.
- SBM prints each available gRPC performance-data endpoint on a separate line,
  including localhost, loopback, hostname, private IP, public IP when detected,
  and the configured port.
- Runtime reservation, lease refresh, launch ownership, cleanup, and shutdown
  are modeled as cohesive state machines. Cleanup cannot retire a runtime still
  owned by another active benchmark.

### Exact nanosecond aggregation with lower SBM overhead

SBM still consumes and aggregates every latency value; SBK 10.6 does not
introduce sampling or approximate percentiles.

- Nanosecond aggregation uses a hybrid paged recorder that groups nearby exact
  latency values while retaining precise counts and global ordering.
- Sparse pages remain compact and promote only when density justifies a direct
  array. Page geometry and sparse promotion limits are configurable and
  validated.
- Periodic windows can release retained cache capacity without shortening the
  reporting interval. Total-window memory policy remains explicit and bounded.
- Recorder selection occurs once during startup, keeping mode decisions out of
  SBM's per-measurement ingestion path.
- Scale tests cover thousands of client batches within one reporting interval,
  and JMH comparisons cover dense, realistic, and adversarial sparse latency
  distributions.

The result is lower sorting, allocation, and retained-memory pressure for
high-cardinality nanosecond workloads while periodic aggregate output remains
responsive.

### Fail-fast SBK, PerL, gRPC, and SBM behavior

- Fixed-record benchmarks can use a validated idle timeout to terminate when
  expected events stop arriving. Duration-based runs retain their established
  behavior.
- Benchmark termination now distinguishes configured completion, requested
  shutdown, EOF, idle timeout, and authoritative failure.
- PerL propagates terminal recorder failures instead of allowing a benchmark to
  appear successful after measurement output has failed.
- Remote gRPC streams surface transport and SBM shutdown failures promptly;
  bounded queues and terminal acknowledgements prevent silent loss or an
  indefinitely blocked remote SBK.
- Writer and reader completion, startup failures, and shutdown failures are
  coordinated without adding new branches, locks, waits, or allocations to
  successful per-record measurement paths.
- Focused JMH gates protect the optimized SBK and PerL hot paths from measurable
  throughput or latency regressions.

### Packaged Java bootstrap for every application

- SBK, SBM, SBK-GEM, SBK-YAL, and SBK-GEM-YAL use explicit Unix and Windows
  launcher templates rather than fragile post-generation script rewriting.
- Each packaged application can opt into the shared Java bootstrap contract and
  reports whether Java came from `SBK_JAVA_HOME`, persisted SBK configuration,
  `JAVA_HOME`, or system discovery.
- The obsolete standalone `install-java` script was removed; wrapper and
  packaged-launcher bootstrap behavior now have one documented implementation.

### Build, test, and release engineering

- The Gradle wrapper is upgraded to 9.7.1 with repository-local build caching,
  configuration caching for routine builds, and faster affected-module checks.
- Root `clean` removes build outputs plus repository-local build and
  configuration caches while preserving shared dependency, wrapper, and
  toolchain downloads under the user's Gradle home.
- Standard Gradle tests print every `PASSED`, `FAILED`, and `SKIPPED` test case.
- Publication staging no longer captures live Gradle projects or tasks during
  execution, eliminating configuration-cache serialization failures.
- `releasecheck -Pprofile=local-docker` runs real two-node SBK-GEM validation
  from Linux and macOS controllers through a disposable Linux controller.
- The release gate covers unit/static checks, bounded-heap queue reclamation,
  Lincheck, JCStress, installed launchers, every logger family, SBM, Web
  Console, YAML launchers, and distributed GEM/GEM-YAL execution.
- Travis CI, JitPack configuration, and obsolete build plumbing were removed.
  Apache RAT license checks remain enforced without the redundant startup
  banner.

### Maintainability improvements

- SBK-GEM's former monolithic benchmark coordinator is decomposed into remote
  environment preparation, deployment transport, runtime policy, lease
  management, workload planning, result printing, and per-node state.
- Full-copy and minimal-copy policies share cache, transfer, verification,
  activation, lifecycle, and cleanup infrastructure without duplicating the
  deployment pipeline.
- Remote path construction uses an explicit platform-independent contract
  rather than scattered string separators.
- Non-driver constants, defaults, filesystem names, timeouts, and orchestration
  limits are centralized in module-owned configuration or focused contracts.

## Compatibility notes

- JDK 25 remains the build/runtime baseline. Wrappers and opted-in packaged
  launchers can provision the pinned JDK when no compatible Java is available.
- SBP remains at major version 4. Distributed SBK clients and SBM must use
  compatible protocol versions.
- SBK-GEM defaults to compact, driver-scoped deployment. Use `-fullcopy true`
  to restore complete-JDK and complete-SBK copying.
- `-runtimecleanup` was replaced by `-packagescleanup`, whose default is
  `true`.
- ChromaDB is not included in the aggregate distribution by default.
- Full SBK `build`, `installDist`, `distTar`, and `distZip` outputs continue to
  contain all enabled drivers, launchers, manifests, and runtime files.

## Installation

1. Download `sbk-10.6.tar` or `sbk-10.6.zip` from this release.
2. Extract it, for example: `tar -xvf sbk-10.6.tar`.
3. Run `<extracted-directory>/bin/sbk -help`.

Standalone SBM and SBK Web Console archives are also attached. Container users
can pull `kmgowda/sbk:10.6` or `ghcr.io/kmgowda/sbk:10.6` after publication.
